title: Child's floor carpet: TSV-free edge-bonded planar memory tiling
idea: As a child asks 'why stack the blocks when the floor is empty?': tile plain, TSV-free DRAM dies edge-to-edge in a ring around the accelerator on a glass panel and join neighbours by sidewall hybrid bonds at 2 um pitch on the polished die edges, forming a planar 'memory carpet' with die-to-die relay links.
why: Kills the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area/bit, 20-30% stack yield loss): commodity-like dies with no TSV keep-out, claimed ~2x bits per wafer versus HBM at ~70% of its bandwidth.

title: Embargoed Soviet engineer's shingled staircase stack with overlap coupling
idea: Under embargo with no TSV etcher or interposer: shingle 8-16 thinned DRAM dies like roof tiles, each overlapping the one below by ~200 um, and pass signals through the overlap by capacitive proximity pads under 1 um of oxide, while power comes in by ordinary wire bonds on the exposed step.
why: Removes TSV drilling, CMP and fine-pitch bonder capex (fixes the HBM TSV tax and capital intensity), using wire-bond-era tools available in U.S. OSATs; ~1 Tb/s per stack at ~0.3 pJ/bit.

title: Farmer's irrigation canals double as mm-wave signal waveguides
idea: A farmer digs one canal for both water and transport: etch microfluidic coolant channels into the interposer, fill them with low-loss dielectric fluid (fluorocarbon) and launch 300 GHz signals down the same channels as dielectric waveguides between memory stacks and logic.
why: Uses one structure for cooling and data movement; claimed 100+ Gb/s per channel over 2-5 cm at <1 pJ/bit, which frees interposer metal layers and lets memory sit farther from the hot die.

title: Biologist's bloodstream: data riding on the stack's power rails
idea: Blood carries oxygen and nutrients in one vessel, so superimpose low-swing, high-frequency data (5-20 GHz OFDM tones) on the HBM power and ground TSVs, which already make up ~50% of TSVs, with on-die LC filters to separate the two.
why: Recovers TSV and bump budget so stacks need fewer dedicated signal TSVs: claimed 30-40% fewer total TSVs, or 1.5x bandwidth for the same TSV count, which cuts the TSV area tax.

title: Alien sees silicon as glass: through-die infrared vertical links
idea: To an alien eye silicon is transparent at 1310 nm. Stack thinned dies with no TSVs and talk vertically with Ge-on-Si micro-photodiodes and tiny modulated emitters or reflectors aimed straight through the silicon bulk, with alignment set by bonding registration.
why: Removes signal TSVs entirely (only power vias remain), so each die gets denser and stack yield rises; dense 10 um optical 'vias' at ~0.2 pJ/bit.

title: 2050 engineer's memory utility: optical DDR pools metered like electricity
idea: In 2050 memory is a metered utility: put commodity DDR dies on co-packaged optical chiplets in a memory sled 1-2 m away and reach it over WDM links at ~1 pJ/bit and ~20 ns of flight time, which replaces most HBM with cheap DRAM shared by many accelerators.
why: Escapes HBM's 3x area/bit and TSV yield loss: claimed 2-3x cheaper bits for capacity-bound AI workloads, plus pooling that cuts stranded memory 25%+.

title: Artist's negative space: SRAM-filled grout bridges between chiplets
idea: An artist paints the empty gaps: fill the 100-500 um dead gaps between HBM stacks and the GPU with thin silicon 'grout' bridge strips that hold repeaters plus 2-8 MB of line-buffer SRAM, so the gap becomes a staging cache and a retiming point.
why: Uses wasted interposer area to absorb bursty traffic and cut DRAM activations (128x overfetch) by ~20%; lower-swing, shorter wire hops cut interface pJ/bit.

title: Postal sorting office in the HBM base die
idea: A postal worker sorts mail by street before delivery: a 2k-entry CAM in the HBM base die holds incoming random 64 B requests for a few hundred ns, sorts them by bank/row and issues one activation per row batch, then scatters the replies back.
why: Attacks destructive read and 128x page overfetch (5.9 pJ per useful bit): claimed 3-6x fewer activations on graph and KV-cache traffic and ~40% lower energy per useful bit.

title: Plumber's two-way pipe: simultaneous bidirectional interposer wires
idea: A plumber's pipe carries flow both ways in a heat exchanger: drive each HBM data wire from both ends at once and cancel your own transmitted signal with a hybrid echo canceller at each receiver, so every wire carries read and write traffic at the same time.
why: Halves the bumps and interposer wires per unit of bandwidth (or doubles bandwidth), which eases the beachfront limit and interposer cost; ~0.4 pJ/bit.

title: Chef's mise en place: command-less, compiler-scheduled streaming DRAM
idea: A chef preps every ingredient before service: for static AI dataflows, the compiler preloads a whole row schedule into the HBM base die, which then streams data open-loop with no per-access command bus, and the freed command/address pins are repurposed as data lanes.
why: Removes command-bus overhead and scheduling bubbles: ~15% more data pins, ~10% more bandwidth efficiency and lower controller periphery power.

title: Beekeeper's honeycomb: hexagonal plasma-diced chiplets for more beachfront
idea: Bees tile with hexagons: plasma-dice compute and memory chiplets into hexagons so each compute die shares three or six full edges with memory dies in a honeycomb mesh, instead of a rectangle with only two usable sides.
why: Raises die-edge beachfront per mm2 by ~1.5-2x, so more memory channels attach per accelerator without TSV stacking: bandwidth per package goes up without HBM's area tax.

title: Weaver's loom: woven wire-and-glass-fiber interposer
idea: A weaver builds strong cloth from crossed threads: weave insulated 10 um copper warp wires and glass-fibre weft into a fabric, laser-weld chosen crossings to make vias, and embed the fabric in glass to form a large-area, lithography-free interposer for memory chiplets.
why: Replaces costly silicon or organic RDL interposers (which need masks and litho) with a textile process; claimed 5-10x cheaper interposer area per cm2 for wide, slow memory buses.

title: Railroad standard gauge: open memory-brick footprint any fab can supply
idea: Railroads boomed once gauge was standard: define an open, royalty-free 'memory brick' footprint (bump map, PHY, thermal envelope, test hooks) so DRAM dies from any fab, including U.S. mature-node lines, drop onto any vendor's interposer the way containers fit any ship.
why: Raises usable supply by breaking HBM's three-vendor lock-in and qualification lag: second-source memory chiplets could add capacity within 18-24 months, not 3-5 years.

title: Submariner's sonar: GHz acoustic pulses through the bonded stack
idea: Sound travels well through solids: put ScAlN thin-film bulk-acoustic transducers on each die and send GHz acoustic pulses vertically through the bonded stack as a contactless data bus, with frequency-division channels assigned per die.
why: TSV-free vertical signalling with no drilled vias, which recovers the TSV area tax and yield loss; speculative 10-50 Gb/s per transducer site at sub-pJ energy.

title: Watchmaker's jewel registration: kinematic self-aligned fine-pitch die stacking
idea: Watchmakers seat parts on jewels and pins: etch V-pyramids and pits into the mating die faces and drop in silica micro-spheres so dies self-register kinematically to <200 nm, which allows 1 um hybrid-bond pitch with cheap pick-and-place tools instead of $5M+ bonders.
why: Cuts the capital intensity of advanced stacking while raising bond density 10x, so more memory bandwidth and dies per stack come from cheaper U.S. OSAT lines.

title: Core-memory technician's threaded coil column broadcast bus
idea: Like wires threaded through a stack of ferrite cores: a single vertical column of aligned on-die spiral coils runs through all 16 dies of a stack, so the base die broadcasts commands and addresses to every die at once inductively, with no command TSVs.
why: Removes command/address TSVs and their keep-out area, so the per-die TSV tax drops and stacks with mismatched dies can be mixed; ~0.1 pJ/bit for broadcast.

title: Origami artist folds one thinned wafer into an accordion stack
idea: Fold rather than stack: process DRAM on a partial wafer thinned to 10 um on a polyimide carrier with continuous RDL running across score lines, then fold it into a zig-zag accordion of 8-16 layers so the inter-layer wiring runs around the folds.
why: No TSVs, no die-to-die bonding and no known-good-die stacking yield multiplication; claimed ~40% lower stacking cost per bit than HBM.

title: Firefighter's bucket brigade: charge-domain CCD data bus on interposer
idea: A bucket brigade passes water hand to hand: move bits across the interposer as packets of charge clocked through CCD-like transfer gates, like a camera readout, instead of charging full wires to rail.
why: Charge transfer needs no full-wire CV2 swing: claimed 5-10x lower energy per bit for long memory buses where data-movement power is 20-25% of the accelerator's.

title: Bedouin water reuse: resonant LC charge recovery on memory buses
idea: A desert nomad never pours water away: place spiral inductors on the interposer that resonate with each memory bus's capacitance, so energy sloshes back and forth between bit transitions instead of being dumped to ground at every edge.
why: Recovers ~60-70% of CV2 bus energy on HBM/DDR links (3-20 pJ/bit today); this is the voltage-floor problem solved in the interface instead of the cell.

title: Cartographer's contour map: exponent-dedupe compression in base die
idea: A map keeps contours, not every pebble: the HBM base die stores and sends AI tensors as per-block shared exponents plus mantissa deltas (BF16/FP8 exponent dedupe), and decompresses at the controller, so fewer bits cross the TSVs and PHY.
why: Claimed 25-40% fewer bits moved and stored for weights and KV-cache, so effective capacity and bandwidth per stack rise by the same factor.

title: Tailor's made-to-measure: maskless late-binding RDL after die test
idea: A tailor cuts after measuring: mount mass-produced memory chiplets loosely, test them, then write the interposer RDL wiring per package with direct-write laser lithography, routing around dead dies and binning good banks into full channels.
why: Removes interposer mask sets and rescues partially failing dies (HBM yield loss 20-30%); claimed 10-15% more usable bits per wafer.

title: Fisherman's net: passive optical multicast of shared weights
idea: One net catches many fish: one memory chiplet's optical transmitter feeds a passive 1:8 splitter, so a shared weight tensor read once from DRAM reaches eight accelerators together instead of being duplicated in eight HBM stacks.
why: Cuts duplicated model copies across GPUs (common in inference serving): claimed 3-8x less DRAM capacity for weights, and one read's energy serves many consumers.

title: Mycologist's fungal network: package-level HBM pooling crossbar
idea: Mycelium lends nutrients between trees: route a switched crossbar through the interposer so that, in a multi-die package, any compute die can borrow idle capacity in a neighbour die's HBM stacks with a one-hop ~5 ns penalty.
why: Reduces stranded HBM (often 20-30% idle per device), so fewer stacks are bought per unit of useful capacity.

title: Soviet vacuum-tube engineer's all-inorganic hermetic memory package
idea: Soviet tubes lasted because they held no organics: build the memory-logic package with zero polymers, using a glass core, Cu-Cu hybrid bonds, CVD SiCN/SiO2 gap-fill instead of underfill and mould, and an anodically bonded glass lid filled with dry nitrogen.
why: Underfill and mould Tg (~110-150 C) and moisture creep are what kill packages at 125 C; going inorganic removes that cliff and lets HBM-class stacks qualify for 10 years at 125 C.

title: Thermophile biologist: fully intermetallic TLP microbumps that cannot age
idea: Thermophilic archaea survive 120 C by using bonds that are already at equilibrium: convert every Cu/Sn microbump completely to Cu3Sn during bonding (transient liquid phase), so no further intermetallic growth or Kirkendall voiding can happen in 10 years at 125 C.
why: Removes the main wear-out mode of memory microbumps at high temperature; lets 25-40 um microbumps survive automotive Grade 0/1 life without hybrid-bonding capex.

title: Venus alien: SiC CMOS base die and memory PHY
idea: For a Venusian 125 C is cold: build the HBM base die and PHY in SiC CMOS (developed for 500 C Venus probes), whose 3.3 eV bandgap keeps leakage negligible at 125 C and whose ~370 W/mK conductivity spreads heat away from the DRAM layers.
why: Hot periphery leakage and timing drift at 125 C go away, and DRAM layers run ~10 C cooler (about 2x less refresh); I/O energy stays flat over temperature.

title: Child's 'mom keeps the flashlight': remote lasers outside the hot zone
idea: Lasers wear out fast at 125 C, so keep them where it is cool: a remote laser bank in a 50 C zone sends CW light over glass fibre, and the 125 C memory package holds only athermal SiN-assisted Mach-Zehnder modulators and Ge detectors, with no light source inside.
why: Allows optical memory links (~1 pJ/bit, cm-to-m reach) in 125 C automotive and industrial packages, so the packages can use remote DRAM instead of soldered-down hot LPDDR.

title: Fresco artist: Taylor-drawn metal-in-glass via plates
idea: Fresco pigment bonds into lime and lasts centuries: draw a bundle of glass tubes filled with copper or silver, as in the Taylor-wire process, into a rod with millions of 5 um metal cores, then slice it into via wafers so the conductors are sealed inside glass with no polymer.
why: Through-glass-via interposers made with no laser drilling or plating, and metal fully encased in stable glass for 125 C/10 year life; claimed 5x cheaper via density than TGV.

title: Farmer's crop rotation: supply TSVs swap VDD and VSS roles
idea: A farmer rotates crops so soil recovers: on-die power switches periodically swap which TSV groups carry VDD and which carry VSS, reversing the DC current direction in each via every few hours so electromigration damage partly heals.
why: Electromigration life falls about 4x from 105 C to 125 C; bipolar stress can extend via life by about 5-10x, so power TSVs can be smaller or fewer at 125 C (less TSV area).

title: Desert architect's double roof: thermal-break gap between memory and logic
idea: Desert dwellers use a ventilated double roof: suspend the DRAM stack over a 5-10 um vacuum gap above the 150 C+ logic die, couple signals across the gap by near-field coupling, and feed power from the board side through separate thermal-choke ribbons.
why: Keeps DRAM at the 125 C ambient instead of logic's 150-170 C junction, cutting refresh about 4-8x and ending retention-driven bandwidth loss.

title: Navy signalman's heliograph: optical retromodulator backscatter from memory
idea: A signalman flashes a mirror instead of carrying a lamp: the cool-side controller shines a beam onto the memory chiplet, which sends data back by switching an electro-absorption retroreflector, so the hot memory side has no laser and very little transmit power.
why: No laser in the 125 C package and almost no transmit heat on the memory side; claimed ~0.2 pJ/bit on the memory end of the link.

title: Japanese swordsmith's folded steel: nanotwinned copper TSVs and bonds
idea: Folded steel is tough because of its layering: plate all TSVs, pillars and hybrid-bond pads as (111) nanotwinned copper, whose twin boundaries block vacancy flow and allow 150-200 C direct bonding.
why: Electromigration life about 10x that of normal Cu at 125 C, and lower bonding temperature limits DRAM retention damage during assembly; this enables 125 C/10 year stacks.

title: Downhole drilling engineer: FD-SOI PHY with temperature-tracking back-bias
idea: Oil-well tools run for years at 175 C on SOI: build the memory interface PHY and base logic on FD-SOI and let an on-die temperature loop set the back-gate bias so threshold voltage, leakage and delay stay constant from -40 C to 150 C.
why: Junction leakage disappears with SOI, and back-bias holds timing and I/O power flat at 125 C, so links run at full speed with no hot derating.

title: Jazz musician plays by ear: self-timed delay-insensitive memory link
idea: A jazz band follows the music, not a metronome: replace the clocked, trained HBM/LPDDR interface with a quasi-delay-insensitive encoding (1-of-4 with acknowledge) whose timing is correct at any temperature, voltage or ageing state, so no retraining is ever needed.
why: Removes timing margin wasted on worst-case 125 C and end-of-life drift, about 20-30% of the link's cycle budget, and skips periodic recalibration stalls over 10 years.

title: Honeybees fan the hive: thin-film thermoelectric cooler under DRAM
idea: Worker bees fan to cool the brood: embed a thin-film Bi2Te3 thermoelectric cooler in the interposer directly under the DRAM stack only, pumping it 15-20 C below the 125 C package while the logic runs hot.
why: DRAM at ~105 C instead of 125 C has about 4x longer retention, so it needs about 4x less refresh energy and loses less bandwidth; the TEC power is spent only on the memory footprint.

title: Sous-vide chef: memory held isothermal at a constant 125 C
idea: Sous-vide works because the temperature never changes: instead of fighting heat, on-die heaters hold the memory stack at a constant 125 C at all times, so it never thermally cycles, and refresh and link timing are calibrated once for that single point.
why: Thermal-cycling fatigue of bumps and interposers, the main packaging failure mode, is eliminated; one-temperature tuning recovers margin that wide-range designs waste.

title: Voyager engineer's lane sparing with lifetime eye-margin remapping
idea: Voyager has run for 49 years on redundancy: add 10% spare lanes, have the base die measure every lane's eye margin weekly and move traffic off lanes that are degrading before they fail, keeping a wear map in on-die fuses.
why: Turns 10 year/125 C bump and TSV wear-out from a fatal event into graceful degradation, which allows fewer, finer-pitch lanes without needing big margins.

title: Potter's kiln: co-fired AlN ceramic memory brick with copper lines
idea: Fired ceramics last millennia: co-fire an aluminium nitride carrier with copper conductors (no tungsten) to form a 'memory brick' that holds 4-8 DRAM dies around a logic die, with a silicon-matched CTE (~4.5 ppm/K) and 170 W/mK conductivity.
why: A rugged 125 C/10 year memory module that avoids China-dominated tungsten and organic laminates, with less thermal-cycle stress than FR-4.

title: Utility lineman's high-voltage lines: 12 V delivery into the stack
idea: Linemen send power at high voltage to cut current: deliver 12 V up a few power TSVs and convert to ~1 V with switched-capacitor converters in the memory base die, cutting the current per power via about 10x.
why: Electromigration scales with current density and degrades steeply at 125 C, so 10x less current lets power-TSV count drop about 70%, freeing area for signals and memory.

title: Horologist's gridiron pendulum: temperature-compensated interconnect delay
idea: A gridiron pendulum pairs brass and steel so their expansion cancels: build skew-critical interposer clock and strobe lines from segments whose delay-temperature coefficients cancel, using a Cu conductor plus a dielectric whose permittivity falls with heat, so skew stays flat from 25 C to 125 C.
why: Removes temperature-driven retraining and guard-band at 125 C, which lets wider, slower links run near their raw limit; about 15% more usable bandwidth when hot.

title: Cathedral builder's flying buttress: corner anchors carrying CTE strain
idea: Flying buttresses carry a wall's thrust outside it: place sintered-silver anchor pillars at the corners and edges of each memory die to take all shear from CTE mismatch, so the fine-pitch signal bonds in the field never see cyclic strain.
why: Fine-pitch signal joints survive 10 years of thermal cycling at 125 C, which allows denser, smaller bonds and so more bandwidth per mm of die edge.

title: Kintsugi artist: liquid-metal microcapsules that heal cracked bonds
idea: Kintsugi fills cracks with gold: embed microcapsules of gallium-indium alloy, with a barrier shell, around microbump fields; when a fatigue crack forms, the capsules break and liquid metal wicks into the gap to restore conduction.
why: Self-repairs interconnect opens during 10 years at 125 C, which extends package life without big redundancy; risky because gallium embrittles Al and Cu.

title: Basking lizard: thermal-aware data migration between memory stacks
idea: A lizard shuttles between sun and shade: the memory controller watches each stack's temperature and moves hot, frequently refreshed pages from the warmest stack to cooler stacks or banks over the interposer, keeping all stacks under their retention limit.
why: At 125 C ambient, hotspots force refresh to double for every ~10 C rise; evening out heat across stacks claims about 2x less refresh overhead.

title: MiG-25 engineer: coarse-pitch mature-node 150 C memory interface
idea: The MiG-25 beat titanium jets with robust steel and tubes: define a 150 C-rated memory chiplet interface using 40 um copper pillars and a 28-65 nm base die built in existing U.S. mature fabs, accepting a bit more energy per bit in return for huge margins.
why: Opens automotive and industrial memory supply to U.S. mature-node fabs and OSATs, with no EUV, and frees leading-edge capacity for AI.

title: Bridge engineer's expansion joints: islands-and-meanders segmented interposer
idea: Long bridges need expansion joints: split a large interposer into rigid silicon islands, one per memory stack and logic die, joined by meandering copper-on-glass bridges that flex, so warpage and CTE stress stay small.
why: Very large memory-rich packages would otherwise warp and crack over 10 years at 125 C; this allows reticle-busting interposers carrying many more stacks.

title: Coal miner's canary: sacrificial early-failure sensors for each memory link
idea: The canary dies first and warns the miners: each package includes intentionally weakened replica bonds, TSVs and lines (narrower, at higher current) that fail first under the same 125 C stress and trigger proactive remapping or service.
why: Gives predictive, calibrated wear-out warning instead of field failures, which allows less over-design (fewer redundant TSVs and less area) while meeting the 10 year/125 C guarantee.
